claim: Low-frequency cortical activity in the delta (<4 Hz) and theta (4–8 Hz) bands is synchronous to speech when listening to speech.
source: When listening to speech, low-frequency cortical activity in the delta (<4 Hz) and theta (4–8 Hz) bands is synchronous to speech (Keitel et al., 2018; Luo and Poeppel, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Keitel et al., 2018; Luo and Poeppel, 2007)

claim: The low-frequency cortical response tracks low-level acoustic features in speech, such as the speech envelope.
source: A large number of studies have demonstrated that the low-frequency cortical response tracks low-level acoustic features in speech, for example, the speech envelope (Destoky et al., 2019; Ding and Simon, 2012; Koskinen and Seppä, 2014; Di Liberto et al., 2015; Nourski et al., 2009; Peelle et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: The theta-band speech envelope provides an important acoustic cue for syllable boundaries.
source: Since the theta-band speech envelope provides an important acoustic cue for syllable boundaries, it has been hypothesized that neural tracking of the theta-band speech envelope is a mechanism to segment continuous speech into discrete units of syllables (Giraud and Poeppel, 2012; Poeppel and Assaneo, 2020).
evidence: Stated as background knowledge with supporting citations

claim: Neural tracking of the theta-band speech envelope is a mechanism to segment continuous speech into discrete units of syllables.
source: Since the theta-band speech envelope provides an important acoustic cue for syllable boundaries, it has been hypothesized that neural tracking of the theta-band speech envelope is a mechanism to segment continuous speech into discrete units of syllables (Giraud and Poeppel, 2012; Poeppel and Assaneo, 2020).
evidence: Presented as a hypothesis supported by citations

claim: The theta-band envelope-tracking response reflects an intermediate neural representation linking auditory representation of acoustic speech features and phonological representation of syllables.
source: In other words, the theta-band envelope-tracking response reflects an intermediate neural representation linking auditory representation of acoustic speech features and phonological representation of syllables.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the hypothesis mentioned in the previous sentence

claim: Neural tracking of speech envelope can occur when speech recognition fails.
source: On one hand, it can occur when speech recognition fails (Etard and Reichenbach, 2019; Howard and Poeppel, 2010; Peña and Melloni, 2012; Zoefel and VanRullen, 2016; Zou et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Neural tracking of speech envelope is strongly modulated by attention.
source: On the other hand, it is strongly modulated by attention (Zion Golumbic et al., 2013; Kerlin et al., 2010) and may be a prerequisite for successful speech recognition (Vanthornhout et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: Neural tracking of speech envelope may be a prerequisite for successful speech recognition.
source: On the other hand, it is strongly modulated by attention (Zion Golumbic et al., 2013; Kerlin et al., 2010) and may be a prerequisite for successful speech recognition (Vanthornhout et al., 2018).
evidence: Presented as a possibility supported by citation

claim: Low-frequency cortical activity can reflect neural processing of higher-level linguistic units, such as words and phrases.
source: Previous studies suggest that low-frequency cortical activity can also reflect neural processing of higher-level linguistic units, for example, words and phrases (Buiatti et al., 2009; Ding et al., 2016a; Keitel et al., 2018), and the prosodic cues related to these linguistic units, for example, delta-band speech envelope and pitch contour (Bourguignon et al., 2013; Li and Yang, 2009; Steinhauer et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Cortical responses can encode word onsets when listening to natural speech.
source: One line of research demonstrates that, when listening to natural speech, cortical responses can encode word onsets (Brodbeck et al., 2018) and capture semantic similarity between words (Broderick et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Cortical responses can capture semantic similarity between words when listening to natural speech.
source: One line of research demonstrates that, when listening to natural speech, cortical responses can encode word onsets (Brodbeck et al., 2018) and capture semantic similarity between words (Broderick et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Cortical responses are synchronous to perceived linguistic units (words, phrases, and sentences) even when acoustic correlates of these linguistic units are not available.
source: These studies demonstrate that cortical responses are synchronous to perceived linguistic units, for example, words, phrases, and sentences, even when acoustic correlates of these linguistic units are not available (Ding et al., 2016a; Ding et al., 2018; Jin et al., 2018; Makov et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Low-frequency cortical activity can reflect linguistic-level neural representations that are constructed based on internal linguistic knowledge instead of acoustic cues.
source: Based on these results, it has been hypothesized that low-frequency cortical activity can reflect linguistic-level neural representations that are constructed based on internal linguistic knowledge instead of acoustic cues (Ding et al., 2016a; Ding et al., 2018; Meyer et al., 2020).
evidence: Presented as a hypothesis with supporting citations

claim: Cortical activity is synchronous to the word rhythm in metrical stories during attentive speech comprehension.
source: These results showed that cortical activity was synchronous to the word rhythm during attentive speech comprehension.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in Figure 2A and Figure 3A

claim: When attention is diverted, the word-rate response is no longer detected.
source: When attention was diverted, however, the word-rate response was no longer detected.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in Figure 2C and Figure 3A

claim: For metrical stories, two peaks were observed in the EEG spectrum at 4 Hz (syllable rate) and 2 Hz (rate of disyllabic words) during the story comprehension task.
source: For metrical stories, two peaks were observed in the EEG spectrum, one at 4 Hz, that is, the syllable rate (p=0.0001, bootstrap, false discovery rate [FDR] corrected) and the other at 2 Hz, that is, the rate of disyllabic words (p=0.0001, bootstrap, FDR corrected).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with statistical significance

claim: For nonmetrical stories, a single response peak was observed at 4 Hz during the story comprehension task, while no significant response peak was observed at 2 Hz.
source: For nonmetrical stories, however, a single response peak was observed at 4 Hz (p=0.0001, bootstrap, FDR corrected), while no significant response peak was observed at 2 Hz (p=0.27, bootstrap, FDR corrected).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with statistical significance

claim: A significant difference was observed at 2 Hz between responses to metrical and nonmetrical stories during the story comprehension task.
source: A comparison of the responses to metrical and nonmetrical stories was performed, and a significant difference was observed at 2 Hz (p=0.0005, bootstrap, FDR corrected, Figure 3A) but not at 4 Hz (p=0.40, bootstrap, FDR corrected, Figure 3B).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with statistical significance

claim: The response topography showed a centro-frontal distribution for the word-rate response.
source: The response topography showed a centro-frontal distribution.
evidence: Observation from experimental data, also visible in topography plots in Figure 2

claim: Participants correctly answered 96 ± 9% and 94 ± 9% questions for metrical and nonmetrical stories, respectively, during the story comprehension task.
source: The task was referred to as story comprehension task, and the participants correctly answered 96 ± 9% and 94 ± 9% questions for metrical and nonmetrical stories, respectively.
evidence: Directly reported behavioral data

claim: Cortical activity was synchronous to the word rhythm in natural spoken narratives during attentive speech comprehension.
source: These results demonstrated that cortical activity was synchronous to the word rhythm in natural spoken narratives during attentive speech comprehension.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in Figure 2E

claim: For metrical stories in natural speech, two peaks were observed in the spectrum of the time-warped response at 4 Hz and 2 Hz.
source: For metrical stories, two peaks were observed in spectrum of the time-warped response, one at 4 Hz (p=0.0002, bootstrap, FDR corrected) and the other at 2 Hz (p=0.0007, bootstrap, FDR corrected).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with statistical significance

claim: For nonmetrical stories in natural speech, a single response peak was observed at 4 Hz, while no significant response peak was observed at 2 Hz.
source: For nonmetrical stories, however, a single response peak was observed at 4 Hz (p=0.0002, bootstrap, FDR corrected), while no significant response peak was observed at 2 Hz (p=0.37, bootstrap, FDR corrected).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with statistical significance

claim: A significant difference was found at 2 Hz between responses to metrical and nonmetrical stories in natural speech.
source: A comparison of the responses to metrical and nonmetrical stories was performed and found a significant difference at 2 Hz (p=0.036, bootstrap, FDR corrected, Figure 3A) but not at 4 Hz (p=0.09, bootstrap, FDR corrected, Figure 3B).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with statistical significance

claim: Amplitude modulation was achieved by amplifying either σ1 or σ2 by a factor of 4.
source: The amplitude modulation (AM) was achieved by amplifying either σ1 or σ2 by a factor of 4 (Figure 1D), creating two conditions: σ1-amplified condition and σ2-amplified condition.
evidence: Description of experimental manipulation, illustrated in Figure 1D

claim: Participants correctly answered 94 ± 12% and 97 ± 8% comprehension questions in the σ1- and σ2-amplified conditions, respectively.
source: When listening to amplitude-modulated speech, the participants correctly answered 94 ± 12% and 97 ± 8% comprehension questions in the σ1- and σ2-amplified conditions, respectively.
evidence: Directly reported behavioral data

claim: Significant response peaks were observed at 2 Hz for both σ1-amplified and σ2-amplified conditions when participants attended to the speech.
source: When participants attended to the speech, significant response peaks were observed at 2 Hz (σ1-amplified: p=0.0001, and σ2-amplified: p=0.0001, bootstrap, FDR corrected, Figure 2D).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with statistical significance

claim: Amplitude modulation did not significantly influence the power of the 2-Hz neural response during attentive speech comprehension.
source: A comparison between the responses to isochronous speech and amplitude-modulated speech found that AM did not significantly influence the power of the 2-Hz neural response (σ1-amplified vs. σ2-amplified: p=0.56; σ1-amplified vs. isochronous: p=0.38, σ2-amplified vs. isochronous: p=0.44, bootstrap, FDR corrected, Figure 3A).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with statistical significance

claim: The 2-Hz response power was not significantly influenced by the 2-Hz AM during attentive speech comprehension.
source: These results showed that the 2-Hz response power was not significantly influenced by the 2- Hz AM during attentive speech comprehension.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from statistical comparisons of experimental data

claim: Significant response peaks were observed at 2 Hz for both σ1-amplified and σ2-amplified conditions during passive listening (movie watching task).
source: In their EEG responses, significant response peaks were also observed at 2 Hz (σ1-amplified: p=0.0001, and σ2-amplified: p=0.0001, bootstrap, FDR corrected, Figure 2D).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with statistical significance

claim: When attention was diverted, the 2-Hz response power was significantly increased by the 2-Hz AM.
source: Therefore, when attention was diverted, the 2-Hz response power was significantly increased by the 2-Hz AM.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from statistical comparisons of experimental data

claim: The 2-Hz response power was significantly stronger in the story comprehension task than in the movie watching task.
source: Furthermore, the 2-Hz response was significantly stronger in the story comprehension task than in the movie watching task (p=0.0004, bootstrap, FDR corrected, Figure 3A).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with statistical significance

claim: The 2-Hz response phase difference between the σ1- and σ2-amplified conditions was 41° during the story comprehension task.
source: The phase difference, when averaged across participants and EEG electrodes, was 41° (95% confidence interval: −25–91°) during the story comprehension task and increased to 132° (95% confidence interval: 102–164°) during the movie watching task (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for response phase in individual conditions).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with confidence intervals

claim: The 2-Hz response phase difference between the σ1- and σ2-amplified conditions was 132° during the movie watching task.
source: The phase difference, when averaged across participants and EEG electrodes, was 41° (95% confidence interval: −25–91°) during the story comprehension task and increased to 132° (95% confidence interval: 102–164°) during the movie watching task (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for response phase in individual conditions).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with confidence intervals

claim: A significant 2-Hz word response was observed during both story comprehension task and movie watching task.
source: For the word response, a significant response peak was observed at 2 Hz during both story comprehension task (p=0.0001, bootstrap, FDR corrected) and movie watching task (p=0.011, bootstrap, FDR corrected, Figure 4B).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with statistical significance

claim: The word response power was significantly stronger in the story comprehension task than in the movie watching task.
source: The response power was significantly stronger in the story comprehension task than that in the movie watching task (p=0.0008, bootstrap, FDR corrected, Figure 4E).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with statistical significance

claim: The 2-Hz AM facilitated word processing during passive listening.
source: This finding indicated that the 2-Hz AM facilitated word processing during passive listening.
evidence: Inference drawn from comparison of word responses to amplitude-modulated vs. isochronous speech during movie watching task

claim: The 2-Hz AM did not significantly modulate the 2-Hz word response during attentive speech comprehension.
source: Furthermore, during the story comprehension task, the power of the 2-Hz word response did not significantly differ between amplitude-modulated speech and isochronous speech (p=0.69, bootstrap, FDR corrected), suggesting that the 2-Hz AM did not significantly modulate the 2-Hz word response during attentive speech comprehension.
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with statistical significance and interpretation

claim: Significant 2-Hz AM response peaks were observed during both the story comprehension task and the movie watching task.
source: For the AM response, significant 2-Hz response peaks were observed during both the story comprehension task (p=0.0021, bootstrap, FDR corrected) and the movie watching task (p=0.0001, bootstrap, FDR corrected).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with statistical significance

claim: The 2-Hz AM response power did not significantly differ between tasks.
source: The 2-Hz response power did not significantly differ between tasks (p=0.39, bootstrap, FDR corrected), suggesting that the 2-Hz AM response was not strongly enhanced when participants attended to speech.
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with statistical significance and interpretation

claim: During the story comprehension task, the 2-Hz response power was significantly stronger for the word response than the AM response.
source: During the story comprehension task, the 2-Hz response power averaged across electrodes was significantly stronger for the word response than the AM response (p=0.021, bootstrap, FDR corrected, Figure 4E).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with statistical significance

claim: During the movie watching task, the 2-Hz word response was significantly weaker than the 2-Hz AM response.
source: During the movie watching task, however, the reverse was true, that is, the 2-Hz word response was significantly weaker than the 2-Hz AM response (p=0.013, bootstrap, FDR corrected, Figure 4E).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with statistical significance

claim: The 2-Hz word and AM responses had distinct neural sources.
source: These results suggested that the 2-Hz word and AM responses had distinct neural sources.
evidence: Inference drawn from topographical differences between word and AM responses

claim: The 2-Hz word response was significantly stronger than the 2-Hz AM response in centro-frontal electrodes during the story comprehension task.
source: An analysis of individual electrodes showed the 2-Hz word response was significantly stronger than the 2-Hz AM response in centro-frontal electrodes during the story comprehension task (p<0.05, bootstrap, FDR corrected, Figure 4F, left).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with statistical significance

claim: Significant difference was found in the normalized topography between the 2-Hz word and AM responses in temporal electrodes.
source: Significant difference was found in the normalized topography between the 2-Hz word and AM responses in temporal electrodes (p<0.05, bootstrap, FDR corrected, Figure 4F, right).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with statistical significance

claim: Participants correctly answered 96 ± 8% and 95 ± 9% questions in the σ1-amplified and σ2-amplified conditions, respectively, in the replication experiment.
source: During the story comprehension task, the participants correctly answered 96 ± 8% and 95 ± 9% questions in the σ1-amplified and σ2-amplified conditions, respectively.
evidence: Directly reported behavioral data from replication experiment

claim: A significant 2-Hz response peak was observed in the replication experiment whether the participants attended to the speech or movie.
source: Consistent with previous results, a significant 2-Hz response peak was observed whether the participants attended to the speech (σ1-amplified: p=0.0001, and σ2-amplified: p=0.0001, bootstrap, FDR corrected) or movie (σ1-amplified: p=0.0001, and σ2-amplified: p=0.0004, bootstrap, FDR corrected, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with statistical significance from replication experiment

claim: The 2-Hz response phase difference between the σ1- and σ2-amplified conditions was 7° during the story comprehension task in the replication experiment.
source: When averaged across participants and electrodes, the 2-Hz response phase difference between the σ1- and σ2-amplified conditions was 7° (95% confidence interval: −26–47°) during the story comprehension task and 96° (95% confidence interval: 55–143°) during the movie watching task (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with confidence intervals from replication experiment

claim: The 2-Hz response phase difference between the σ1- and σ2-amplified conditions was 96° during the movie watching task in the replication experiment.
source: When averaged across participants and electrodes, the 2-Hz response phase difference between the σ1- and σ2-amplified conditions was 7° (95% confidence interval: −26–47°) during the story comprehension task and 96° (95% confidence interval: 55–143°) during the movie watching task (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with confidence intervals from replication experiment

claim: A significant 2-Hz word response was observed during both tasks in the replication experiment.
source: Similar to previous results, in the spectrum (Figure 5A and B), a significant 2-Hz word response was observed during both tasks (story comprehension task: p=0.0001, bootstrap; movie watching task: p=0.0003, bootstrap, FDR corrected), and a significant 2-Hz AM response was also observed during both tasks (story comprehension task: p=0.0001, bootstrap; movie watching task: p=0.0001, bootstrap, FDR corrected).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with statistical significance from replication experiment

claim: The 2-Hz word response exhibited significantly stronger power than the 2-Hz AM response during the story comprehension task in the replication experiment.
source: Furthermore, the 2-Hz word response exhibited significantly stronger power than the 2-Hz AM response during the story comprehension task (p=0.0036, bootstrap, FDR corrected, Figure 5C), and the two responses showed distinct topographical distribution (Figure 5D).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with statistical significance from replication experiment

claim: The 2-Hz word response exhibited significantly stronger power during the movie watching task in the replication experiment than the original experiment.
source: A follow-up comparison of the results from the original and replication experiments suggested that the 2-Hz word response exhibited significantly stronger power during the movie watching task in the replication experiment than the original experiment (p=0.0008, bootstrap, FDR corrected).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with statistical significance comparing two experiments

claim: The ERP responses to σ1 and σ2 showed significant differences for both isochronous and natural speech when participants attended to speech.
source: When participants attended to speech, the ERP responses to σ1 and σ2 showed significant differences for both isochronous (Figure 6A) and natural speech (Figure 6B).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with reference to figures

claim: A smaller difference was observed between the ERP responses to σ1 and σ2 when participants watched a silent movie.
source: When participants watched a silent movie, a smaller difference was also observed between the ERP responses to σ1 and σ2 (Figure 6A).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with reference to figure

claim: The topography of the ERP difference showed a centro-frontal distribution.
source: The topography of the ERP difference showed a centro-frontal distribution.
evidence: Observation from experimental data, visible in topography plots in Figure 6

claim: For natural speech, the ERP responses to σ1 and σ2 differed in a time window around 300–500 ms.
source: For natural speech, the ERP responses to σ1 and σ2 differed in a time window around 300–500 ms.
evidence: Directly reported experimental results

claim: When participants attended to speech, a difference between the ERP responses to σ1 and σ2 was observed in both σ1- and σ2-amplified conditions.
source: When participants attended to speech, a difference between the ERP responses to σ1 and σ2 was observed in both σ1- and σ2-amplified conditions (Figure 6C).
evidence: Directly reported experimental results with reference to figure

claim: During passive listening, a significant ERP difference was observed near the onset of the amplified syllable.
source: During passive listening, however, a significant ERP difference was observed near the onset of the amplified syllable.
evidence: Directly reported experimental results

claim: Bottom-up acoustic cues and top-down linguistic knowledge separately contribute to word synchronous neural responses.
source: In sum, these results show that both top-down linguistic knowledge and bottom-up acoustic cues separately contribute to word synchronous neural responses.
evidence: Overall conclusion drawn from all experimental results

claim: Bottom-up acoustic cues and top-down linguistic knowledge separately contribute to cortical encoding of linguistic units in spoken narratives.
source: These results suggest that bottom-up acoustic cues and top-down linguistic knowledge separately contribute to cortical encoding of linguistic units in spoken narratives.
evidence: Overall conclusion stated in the abstract

claim: Neural activity synchronous to multi-syllabic words is observed when participants naturally listen to narratives.
source: Here we investigate the neural encoding of words using electroencephalography and observe neural activity synchronous to multi-syllabic words when participants naturally listen to narratives.
evidence: Main finding stated in the abstract

claim: An amplitude modulation (AM) cue for word rhythm enhances the word-level response, but the effect is only observed during passive listening.
source: An amplitude modulation (AM) cue for word rhythm enhances the word-level response, but the effect is only observed during passive listening.
evidence: Main finding stated in the abstract

claim: Words and the AM cue are encoded by spatially separable neural responses that are differentially modulated by attention.
source: Furthermore, words and the AM cue are encoded by spatially separable neural responses that are differentially modulated by attention.
evidence: Main finding stated in the abstract

claim: Sixty-eight participants took part in the EEG experiments.
source: Sixty-eight participants (20–29 years old, mean age, 22.6 years; 37 females) took part in the EEG experiments.
evidence: Directly reported participant information

claim: Thirty-four participants took part in a behavioral test to assess the naturalness of the stimuli.
source: Thirty-four participants (19–26 years old, mean age, 22.5 years; 17 females) took part in a behavioral test to assess the naturalness of the stimuli.
evidence: Directly reported participant information

claim: All participants were right-handed native Mandarin speakers, with no self-reported hearing loss or neurological disorders.
source: All participants were right-handed native Mandarin speakers, with no self-reported hearing loss or neurological disorders.
evidence: Directly reported participant information

claim: Twenty-eight short stories were constructed for the study.
source: Twenty-eight short stories were constructed for the study.
evidence: Directly reported stimulus information

claim: In 21 stories, word onset was metrically organized and every other syllable was a word onset (metrical stories).
source: In 21 stories, word onset was metrically organized and every other syllable was a word onset, and these stories were referred to as metrical stories (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly reported stimulus design information

claim: In seven stories, word onset was not metrically organized (nonmetrical stories).
source: In the other seven stories, word onset was not metrically organized and these stories were referred to as nonmetrical stories (Figure 1B).
evidence: Directly reported stimulus design information

claim: For σ2 syllables in metrical stories, 77% was the second syllable of a disyllabic word while 23% was a monosyllabic word.
source: The parsing result confirmed that every other syllable in the story (referred to as σ1 in Figure 1A) was the onset of a word. For the other syllables (referred to as σ2 in Figure 1A), 77% was the second syllable of a disyllabic word while 23% was a monosyllabic word.
evidence: Directly reported stimulus composition information

claim: All syllables in isochronous speech were adjusted to 250 ms duration.
source: All syllables were adjusted to 250 ms by truncation or padding silence at the end, following the procedure in Ding et al., 2016a.
evidence: Directly reported stimulus preparation procedure

claim: Syllables in isochronous speech were presented at a constant rate of 4 Hz.
source: In this way, the syllables were presented at a constant rate of 4 Hz (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Directly reported stimulus presentation rate

claim: A silence gap lasting 500 ms was inserted at the position of any punctuation in isochronous speech.
source: In addition, a silence gap lasting 500 ms, that is, the duration of two syllables, was inserted at the position of any punctuation, to facilitate story comprehension.
evidence: Directly reported stimulus design detail

claim: The total duration of natural speech was 1122 s for the 21 metrical stories and 372 s for the seven nonmetrical stories.
source: The total duration of speech was 1122 s for the 21 metrical stories and 372 s for the seven nonmetrical stories.
evidence: Directly reported stimulus duration information

claim: Most participants did not perceive any difference between the metrical and nonmetrical stories.
source: A behavioral test showed that most participants did not perceive any difference between the metrical and nonmetrical stories (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Directly reported behavioral test results

claim: In σ1-amplified condition, all σ1 syllables were amplified by a factor of 4.
source: In σ1-amplified condition, all σ1 syllables were amplified by a factor of 4.
evidence: Directly reported stimulus manipulation procedure

claim: In σ2-amplified condition, all σ2 syllables were amplified by a factor of 4.
source: In σ2-amplified condition, all σ2 syllables were amplified by a factor of 4.
evidence: Directly reported stimulus manipulation procedure

claim: Sound intensity is a weak cue for stress.
source: Such 2-Hz AM was clearly perceivable but did not affect speech intelligibility, since sound intensity is a weak cue for stress (Zhong et al., 2001) and stress does not affect word recognition in Mandarin Chinese (Duanmu, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Stress does not affect word recognition in Mandarin Chinese.
source: Such 2-Hz AM was clearly perceivable but did not affect speech intelligibility, since sound intensity is a weak cue for stress (Zhong et al., 2001) and stress does not affect word recognition in Mandarin Chinese (Duanmu, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Thirty-one participants (91%) reported no difference perceived between metrical and nonmetrical stories in the behavioral test.
source: Thirty-one participants (91%) reported no difference perceived, and the other three participants (9%) were asked to elaborate on the differences they detected.
evidence: Directly reported behavioral test results

claim: Twenty-four participants (71%) reported that both types of stories were naturally read.
source: Twenty-four participants (71%) reported that both the two types of stories were naturally read.
evidence: Directly reported behavioral test results

claim: Fifteen participants (44%) perceived σ1-amplified speech as being more natural.
source: Fifteen participants (44%) perceived σ1-amplified speech as being more natural, two participants (6%) perceived the σ2-amplified speech as being more natural, and the rest 17 participants (50%) thought there was no difference in naturalness between the two conditions.
evidence: Directly reported behavioral test results

claim: Experiments 1–3 involved 16 participants each, and Experiment 4 involved 20 participants.
source: Experiments 1–3 involved 16 participants respectively, and Experiment 4 involved 20 participants.
evidence: Directly reported participant information for each experiment

claim: 87.5% participants (N = 14) in Experiment 2 reported that they did not notice any story during the movie watching task.
source: The experiment was followed up with questions on the awareness of stories being presented during the movie watching task, and 87.5% participants (N = 14) reported that they did not notice any story.
evidence: Directly reported behavioral data from Experiment 2

claim: 15% participants (N = 3) in Experiment 4 reported that they did not notice any story during the movie watching task.
source: Block 1 was followed up with questions on the awareness of stories being presented during the movie watching task, and 15% participants (N = 3) reported that they did not notice any story during the task.
evidence: Directly reported behavioral data from Experiment 4

claim: The percentage of participants reporting no awareness of the presentation of stories was much lower in Experiment 4 than in Experiment 2.
source: Note that the percentage of participants reporting no awareness of the presentation of stories was much lower in Experiment 4 than that in Experiment 2.
evidence: Comparison of behavioral data between experiments

claim: Experiment 4 only presented amplitude-modulated speech and the consistent presence of word-rate acoustic cues facilitated word recognition.
source: A potential explanation was that Experiment 4 only presented amplitude-modulated speech and the consistent presence of word-rate acoustic cues facilitated word recognition.
evidence: Proposed explanation for difference in awareness between experiments

claim: In Experiment 2, the lack of consistent presence of AM cue diminished its effect.
source: In Experiment 2, however, as amplitude-modulated speech was mixed with isochronous speech, the lack of consistent presence of AM cue diminished its effect.
evidence: Proposed explanation for difference in awareness between experiments

claim: Sixty-four EEG electrodes were recorded.
source: Sixty-four EEG electrodes were recorded.
evidence: Directly reported data acquisition information

claim: The EEG/EOG recordings were low-pass filtered below 400 Hz and sampled at 2048 Hz.
source: The EEG/EOG recordings were low-pass filtered below 400 Hz and sampled at 2048 Hz.
evidence: Directly reported data acquisition parameters

claim: The EEG recordings were down-sampled to 128 Hz.
source: The EEG recordings were down-sampled to 128 Hz, referenced to the average of mastoid recordings, and band-pass filtered between 0.8 Hz and 30 Hz using a linear-phase finite impulse response (FIR) filter (6 s Hamming window, −6 dB attenuation at the cut-off frequencies).
evidence: Directly reported data preprocessing procedure

claim: On average, 8.45 ± 3.20% trials were rejected in Experiment 1.
source: On average, 8.45 ± 3.20% trials were rejected in Experiment 1, 15.20% ± 3.97% trials were rejected in Experiment 2, 10.35% ± 1.53% trials were rejected in Experiment 3, and 12.9 ± 4.46% trials were rejected in Experiment 4.
evidence: Directly reported data quality information

claim: The frequency resolution of the DFT analysis was 1/7 Hz.
source: Therefore, the frequency resolution of the DFT analysis was 1/7 Hz.
evidence: Directly reported analysis parameter

claim: The 400 ms latency response observed in the current study is consistent with the latency of the N400 response.
source: In natural speech, the responses to the two syllables in a disyllabic word differ in a late latency window of about 400 ms. This component is consistent with the latency of the N400 response, which can be observed when listening to either individual words or continuous speech (Broderick et al., 2018; Kutas and Federmeier, 2011; Kutas and Hillyard, 1980; Pylkkänen and Marantz, 2003; Pylkkänen et al., 2002).
evidence: Comparison of current results with previous literature

claim: The N400 is related to lexical processing.
source: The 400 ms latency response observed in the current study is consistent with the hypothesis that the N400 is related to lexical processing (Friederici, 2002; Kutas and Federmeier, 2011).
evidence: Interpretation of results based on cited literature

claim: The second syllable in a disyllabic word may elicit weaker N400 since it is more predictable than the first syllable.
source: Besides, it is also possible that the second syllable in a disyllabic word elicits weaker N400 since it is more predictable than the first syllable (Kuperberg et al., 2020; Lau et al., 2008).
evidence: Alternative explanation proposed with supporting citations

claim: The difference between the ERPs evoked by the first and second syllables in disyllabic words was amplified by attention.
source: The difference between the ERPs evoked by the first and second syllables in disyllabic words was amplified by attention (Figure 6A).
evidence: Observation from experimental data

claim: Word-level processing occurs during the movie watching task, but the word-tracking response is rather weak.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that word-level processing occurs during the movie watching task, but the word-tracking response is rather weak.
evidence: Inference drawn from comparison of ERP and spectral results

claim: Cortical tracking of speech strongly depends on the listeners' task.
source: Finally, since previous studies have shown that cortical tracking of speech strongly depended on the listeners' task (Ding and Simon, 2012; Zion Golumbic et al., 2013; O'Sullivan et al., 2015), we designed two tasks during which the neural responses were recorded.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Strict periodicity in the stimulus could boost rhythmic neural entrainment.
source: A comparison of the responses to natural speech and isochronous speech showed that responses to word and syllable were weaker for natural speech, suggesting that strict periodicity in the stimulus could indeed boost rhythmic neural entrainment.
evidence: Inference drawn from comparison of responses to natural and isochronous speech

claim: Low-frequency word-rate neural response more strongly reflects neural processing of novel words, instead of the perception of a steady rhythm.
source: Therefore, it is possible that low-frequency word-rate neural response more strongly reflects neural processing of novel words, instead of the perception of a steady rhythm (see also Ostarek et al., 2020).
evidence: Proposed explanation for differences between studies, with supporting citation

claim: Syntax has a significant impact on prosody perception.
source: Previous psycholinguistic studies have already demonstrated that syntax has a significant impact on prosody perception (Buxó-Lugo and Watson, 2016; Garrett et al., 1966).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Neural processing associated with temporal prediction may appear to be synchronous to the perceived linguistic units.
source: For example, within a word, later syllables are more predictable that earlier syllables. Therefore, neural processing associated with temporal prediction (Breska and Deouell, 2017; Lakatos et al., 2013; Stefanics et al., 2010) may appear to be synchronous to the perceived linguistic units.
evidence: Proposed explanation with supporting citations

claim: When the predictability of syllables is controlled as a constant, cortical activity can still synchronize to perceived artificial words.
source: However, it has been demonstrated that when the predictability of syllables is controlled as a constant, cortical activity can still synchronize to perceived artificial words, suggesting that temporal prediction is not the only factor driving low-frequency neural activity either (Ding et al., 2016a).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Temporal prediction is not the only factor driving low-frequency neural activity.
source: However, it has been demonstrated that when the predictability of syllables is controlled as a constant, cortical activity can still synchronize to perceived artificial words, suggesting that temporal prediction is not the only factor driving low-frequency neural activity either (Ding et al., 2016a).
evidence: Inference drawn from cited study

claim: Temporal attention is known to affect low-frequency activity.
source: Similarly, temporal attention is known to affect low-frequency activity and attention certainly varies during speech perception (Astheimer and Sanders, 2009; Jin et al., 2018; Sanders and Neville, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Low-frequency neural activity has been suggested to reflect the perception of high-level rhythms.
source: In addition, low-frequency neural activity has also been suggested to reflect the perception of high-level rhythms (Nozaradan et al., 2011) and general sequence chunking (Jin et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Low-frequency neural activity has been suggested to reflect general sequence chunking.
source: In addition, low-frequency neural activity has also been suggested to reflect the perception of high-level rhythms (Nozaradan et al., 2011) and general sequence chunking (Jin et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: The low-frequency response to natural speech is likely to be a mixture of multiple components.
source: Since multiple factors can drive low-frequency neural responses, the low-frequency response to natural speech is likely to be a mixture of multiple components, including, for example, auditory responses to acoustic prosodic features, neural activity related to temporal prediction and temporal attention, and neural activity encoding phonological, syntactic, or semantic information.
evidence: Inference drawn from discussion of multiple contributing factors

claim: The word-rate response may provide a reference signal to bind together mental representations of multiple dimensions of the same word.
source: It may well consist of a mixture of multiple response components, or provide a reference signal to bind together mental representations of multiple dimensions of the same word.
evidence: Proposed hypothesis about the function of word-rate response

claim: Temporal coherence between neural responses to different features provides a strong cue to bind these features into a perceived object.
source: It has been suggested that temporal coherence between neural responses to different features provides a strong cue to bind these features into a perceived object (Shamma et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: The word-rate response may reflect the temporal coherence between distinct mental representations of each word and functionally relate to the binding of these representations.
source: It is possible that the word-rate response reflects the temporal coherence between distinct mental representations of each word and functionally relates to the binding of these representations.
evidence: Proposed hypothesis about the function of word-rate response

claim: Prosodic cues have a facilitative effect on speech comprehension.
source: This result is consistent with the idea that prosodic cues have a facilitative effect on speech comprehension (Frazier et al., 2006; Ghitza, 2017; Ghitza, 2020; Giraud and Poeppel, 2012).
evidence: Interpretation of results consistent with cited literature

claim: The AM is only a weak prosodic cue compared with other variables such as timing and pitch contour.
source: However, the AM is only a weak prosodic cue compared with other variables such as timing and pitch contour (Shen, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Cortical tracking of speech is strongly modulated by attention in a complex auditory scene consisting of two speakers.
source: Most previous studies demonstrate that in a complex auditory scene consisting of two speakers, attention can selectively enhance neural tracking of attended speech (Ding and Simon, 2012; Zion Golumbic et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The auditory cortex can parse a complex auditory scene into auditory objects and separately represent each auditory object.
source: These results strongly suggest that the auditory cortex can parse a complex auditory scene into auditory objects, for example, speakers, and separately represent each auditory object (Shamma et al., 2011; Shinn-Cunningham, 2008).
evidence: Inference drawn from previous studies with supporting citations

claim: When only one speech stream was presented, cross-modal attention can modulate neural tracking of the speech envelope, but the effect is much weaker.
source: When only one speech stream was presented, cross-modal attention can also modulate neural tracking of the speech envelope, but the effect is much weaker (Ding et al., 2018; Kong et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The 4-Hz syllable response was enhanced by cross-modal attention.
source: Consistent with previous findings, in the current study, the 4-Hz syllable response was also enhanced by cross-modal attention (Figure 3B).
evidence: Observation from experimental data consistent with previous findings

claim: Attention did not uniformly enhance the processing of all features within the same speech stream.
source: The 2-Hz AM response power, however, was not significantly modulated by cross-modal attention (Figures 4D and 5B), suggesting that attention did not uniformly enhance the processing of all features within the same speech stream.
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental data

claim: Attention selectively enhances speech features relevant to speech comprehension.
source: Given that the 2-Hz AM does not carry linguistic information, the result suggests that attention selectively enhances speech features relevant to speech comprehension.
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental data

claim: Early ERP components, such as the N1, mostly reflect auditory encoding of acoustic features.
source: Early ERP components, such as the N1, mostly reflect auditory encoding of acoustic features, while late components can reflect higher-level processing of lexical, semantic, or syntactic processing (Friederici, 2002; Friederici, 2012; Sanders and Neville, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Late ERP components can reflect higher-level processing of lexical, semantic, or syntactic processing.
source: Early ERP components, such as the N1, mostly reflect auditory encoding of acoustic features, while late components can reflect higher-level processing of lexical, semantic, or syntactic processing (Friederici, 2002; Friederici, 2012; Sanders and Neville, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: For isochronous speech, response latency cannot be uniquely determined.
source: In the current study, for isochronous speech, response latency cannot be uniquely determined: Given that syllables are presented at a constant rate of 4 Hz, a response with latency T cannot be distinguished from responses with latency T ± 250 ms.
evidence: Logical inference from the periodic nature of the stimulus

claim: The responses observed for isochronous speech could turn out to be predictive instead of reactive.
source: The periodic pattern in the stimulus design enables accurate prediction of its timing in the brain, and therefore the responses observed could turn out to be predictive instead of reactive.
evidence: Inference about the nature of responses to periodic stimuli

claim: The initial syllable of an English word elicits larger N1 and N200–300 components than the word-medial syllable.
source: A previous study on the neural responses to naturally spoken sentences has also shown that the initial syllable of an English word elicits larger N1 and N200–300 components than the word-medial syllable (Sanders and Neville, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: The word onset in natural speech elicits a response at ~100 ms latency.
source: A recent study also suggests that the word onset in natural speech elicits a response at ~100 ms latency (Brodbeck et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: The current study does not observe an early effect at ~100 ms latency.
source: The current study, however, does not observe this early effect, and language difference might offer a potential explanation: In Chinese, a syllable generally equals a morpheme, while in English single syllables do not carry meaning in most cases.
evidence: Observation from current study with proposed explanation

claim: In Chinese, a syllable generally equals a morpheme.
source: In Chinese, a syllable generally equals a morpheme, while in English single syllables do not carry meaning in most cases.
evidence: Statement of linguistic knowledge

claim: In English, single syllables do not carry meaning in most cases.
source: In Chinese, a syllable generally equals a morpheme, while in English single syllables do not carry meaning in most cases.
evidence: Statement of linguistic knowledge
